name: Ipilimumab
route_note: IV infusion, typically 4 doses every 3 weeks alone or with nivolumab, or every 6 weeks in some combinations

discovery.by: James P. Allison and colleagues (University of California, Berkeley)
discovery.note: Showed that antibody blockade of CTLA-4 causes rejection of tumours in mice; ipilimumab is a fully human IgG1 made in Medarex transgenic mice.

tagline: First immune checkpoint inhibitor, releasing the CTLA-4 brake on T cells
summary: Ipilimumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that blocks CTLA-4, an inhibitory receptor on T cells. In 2011 it became the first drug shown to prolong survival in metastatic melanoma and the first immune checkpoint inhibitor approved; it is now used mostly in combination with nivolumab.
mechanism: CTLA-4 is upregulated on activated T cells and outcompetes the costimulatory receptor CD28 for the ligands CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, dampening T-cell priming. Regulatory T cells express CTLA-4 constitutively.

Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, enhancing T-cell activation and proliferation in lymphoid tissue and broadening the anti-tumour T-cell response; it may also deplete intratumoural regulatory T cells through Fc-mediated mechanisms. The same disinhibition causes immune-related adverse events.
uses: Unresectable or metastatic melanoma (alone or with nivolumab)
Hepatocellular carcinoma, non-small cell lung cancer and pleural mesothelioma (with nivolumab)

history.title: CTLA-4 blockade concept
history.detail: Allison's group reports tumour rejection in mice treated with anti-CTLA-4 antibody.

history.title: Survival benefit
history.detail: A phase 3 trial (Hodi et al.) shows improved overall survival in previously treated metastatic melanoma.

history.title: FDA approval
history.detail: Approved in March as Yervoy, the first immune checkpoint inhibitor.

history.title: Combination with nivolumab
history.detail: FDA approves nivolumab plus ipilimumab for metastatic melanoma.

history.title: Adjuvant melanoma
history.detail: Approved for adjuvant treatment of resected stage III melanoma.

history.title: Nobel Prize
history.detail: James Allison shares the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Tasuku Honjo for cancer therapy by inhibiting negative immune regulation.

history.title: Renal cell carcinoma
history.detail: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab approved for intermediate/poor-risk advanced RCC (CheckMate 214).

pk.metabolism: Proteolytic catabolism to peptides and amino acids (no CYP metabolism)
pk.excretion: Not renally excreted as intact antibody; cleared by catabolism and target-mediated uptake

serious: Immune-mediated endocrinopathies (thyroiditis, hypophysitis, adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes)

facts: Ipilimumab causes more frequent severe immune-related adverse events than PD-1 inhibitors, especially colitis and hypophysitis.
Its approval was a landmark in establishing cancer immunotherapy, rewarded by the 2018 Nobel Prize to James Allison.
